subject: typewriter
pitch: A 1930s typewriter in glossy racing green. Round keys with cream letters on chrome rims in four staggered rows, a semicircle of thin type bars behind them, a chrome carriage return lever, a black platen roller with a sheet of paper half typed, and a small brass maker's badge on the front.

Now I'm picturing the model itself: a 1930s-style typewriter, roughly 40cm wide, 30cm deep, 20cm tall, standing on y=0 and facing +Z toward the user. I'm also thinking through the typebar basket, a fan-shaped semicircle converging on the platen's strike point, and the overall body shape—a boxy frame with a sloped keyboard, staggered key rows (numbers, QWERTY, ASDF, ZXCV), and round keys with chrome rims and cream lettering per the user's request.

I'll add a chrome carriage-return lever on the right side with a sweeping arc and knob, a black platen roller at the top-back with end knobs, and a paper sheet wrapped around it showing typed text lines rendered via SVG.

For the brass maker's badge, I'm thinking of a small plate with engraved-looking text like "HARTWELL & CO. — PORTABLE NO. 5", using an SVG texture with a gold gradient so it reads as drawn with colour. For the glossy racing green body, I'm leaning toward British racing green (#004225) and wondering how to control roughness per part since the API seems to only expose plain color strings.

Since true gloss control isn't directly available, I'm considering faking a specular sheen with a painted highlight band that brightens where surfaces face upward, mimicking a glossy highlight. I'm also weighing whether to bypass the builder and add a raw three.js mesh with a custom material directly to a joint, though that risks breaking the rule that all geometry should go through the builder.

Since a typewriter is static, riding the root joint works fine for props. Though the instructions do allow plain objects without joints for props and scenery, using the builder's joint system is the safer path since paints and baking only apply through builder meshes — so I'll set up a single root "base" joint at the origin and attach everything to it, letting `b.part` default to that nearest joint.

For moving parts though, it's worth giving them their own joints: a hinge-role joint for the carriage return lever, and maybe one for the platen/carriage assembly. I'll keep the rest of the body static under the root joint rather than over-engineering joints for every key.

I'm sketching out concrete dimensions for a 1930s desktop typewriter — roughly 0.42m wide, 0.36m deep, with the body housing sitting low and the carriage rising to about 0.22m at the back, sloping down toward the keyboard well at front.
